lead: A sensor output is a number, and a number means nothing until two people agree what it counts. Units give that agreement; standards give a physical reference; calibration connects the two. This chapter runs the chain from the SI units down through primary, secondary and working standards to the instrument on a plant floor or a hospital ward, and ends with the static calibration procedure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 on what the sensor is converting, so that the input unit and the output unit are both clear before you compare them.

blocks.text: A number stays useless until everyone agrees on the size of the unit. The SI has seven base units: the metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).
Since 20 May 2019 each base unit is fixed by giving an exact value to a constant of nature, so any well-equipped laboratory can realise it:

head: Unit
Fixed by the exact value of
rows: luminous efficacy of 540 THz light, 683 lm/W

blocks.text: Every other unit on a datasheet is built from these. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²; 1 Pa = 1 N/m²; 1 V = 1 kg·m²/(s³·A); 1 Ω = 1 V/A; 1 F = 1 C/V; 1 Hz = 1/s. The degree Celsius is a shifted kelvin: t(°C) = T(K) − 273.15, so a temperature difference of 1 °C equals 1 K, but 20 °C is 293.15 K, not 20 K.

Two habits catch most errors. Write the unit beside every number. Run a dimensional check: sensitivity = output unit ÷ input unit. A pressure sensor giving 19.9 mV/kPa has the dimensions of voltage per pressure (V/Pa); the numerical value changes with the unit, the dimension does not. To convert 0.137 V/psi to V/kPa, divide by 6.89476 kPa/psi: S = 0.137 V/psi ÷ 6.89476 kPa/psi = 0.0199 V/kPa = 19.9 mV/kPa. To go the other way (mV/kPa → mV/psi), multiply by 6.89476. Rule: multiply by the ratio that cancels the old unit, and check direction: 1 psi is bigger than 1 kPa, so a sensitivity per psi is a bigger number than per kPa.

sections.h3: The ladder of standards and traceability

blocks.text: You cannot check a volt against nature on a shop floor. So the world uses a ladder, and every rung is calibrated against the rung above it.

items: International: the BIPM, near Paris, coordinates the SI and the key comparisons between national institutes.

Primary: the national standards, kept by the national metrology institute (in India, CSIR–National Physical Laboratory, New Delhi). They realise the SI units directly, for example a caesium clock or a Josephson voltage array, and are used only to calibrate secondary standards, never for routine work.

Secondary: standard resistors, Zener voltage references, gauge blocks and standard weights held by accredited calibration laboratories and checked against the primary standards. Some syllabi call this rung the reference standard.
Working: the dead-weight tester, decade box or process calibrator in a plant or hospital workshop, checked against a secondary standard and used every day on field instruments.

blocks.text: Each rung is more accurate than the one below, typically by a factor of four to ten; a standard only as good as the device under test proves nothing. A hospital’s biomedical engineering team works on the bottom rungs: it checks a patient monitor’s pressure channel against a calibrated digital manometer and its temperature channel against a reference thermometer in a stirred bath.

Traceability is what makes the ladder usable: an unbroken chain of calibrations, each link with a stated uncertainty, each documented, ending at a primary standard. A sensor is traceable when you can show that chain with certificates, uncertainties and dates. Traceability does not make an instrument accurate; it makes its error known and comparable.

sections.h3: Calibration, verification, adjustment, and the static procedure

blocks.text: Calibration compares the instrument output with a known input produced by a standard, and records the result. It is a measurement and a record; it need not change anything. Verification is a pass/fail check: is the reading inside the allowed limits? Adjustment is the physical turning of the zero and span trims so the output matches the ideal line. You adjust after you calibrate, then calibrate again to prove the adjustment worked.

items: Hold other inputs constant — temperature, supply voltage, mounting torque, vibration — and record them; they belong on the certificate.
Pick five to ten input values over the range, including both ends.
Apply them going up (up-scale); record the output at each point.
Apply them going down (down-scale); record again. The largest gap at the same input is the hysteresis.
Fit a straight line: the end-point line joining the extremes, or a least-squares line.
Read sensitivity (slope), zero offset (intercept), non-linearity (largest deviation from the line) and hysteresis.
Write the certificate: range, sensitivity, zero offset, hysteresis, uncertainty, conditions held, standard used and its traceability, date.

blocks.text: In this book %FS means a percentage of the full-scale output span: output at the upper limit minus output at the lower limit (3.98 V in the example). Some datasheets divide by the upper-limit output (4.00 V) instead; for a small zero offset only the third figure changes. The static numbers are defined in static characteristics; repeated-reading uncertainty in error analysis.

spec.aria: Top: five boxes in a row, SI units fixed by constants, primary standard at the national institute, secondary standard at a calibration lab, working standard the dead-weight tester, and the 0 to 200 kilopascal sensor. Below: deviation from the end-point line in millivolts against pressure; up-scale points 0, minus 5, minus 30, plus 15, 0; down-scale points 10, 15, 10, 35, 0; the 40 millivolt gap at 100 kilopascals is marked as hysteresis.

examples.question: A 0–200 kPa pressure sensor is calibrated against a dead-weight tester with temperature held at 25 °C and supply at 10 V. Up-scale, pressures 0, 50, 100, 150, 200 kPa give 0.02, 1.01, 1.98, 3.02, 4.00 V; down-scale, the same pressures give 0.03, 1.03, 2.02, 3.04, 4.00 V. Find the end-point sensitivity, the zero offset, the largest deviation of the up-scale curve from the end-point line, and the hysteresis, each as %FS.
steps: End-point sensitivity S = (4.00 − 0.02) V ÷ 200 kPa = 3.98 V ÷ 200 kPa = 0.0199 V/kPa = 19.9 mV/kPa.
Zero offset = output at zero input = 0.02 V. Output span = 4.00 − 0.02 = 3.98 V.
End-point line: V<sub>ideal</sub> = 0.02 + 0.0199 × P, with V in volts and P in kPa. The table gives V<sub>ideal</sub>, the up-scale deviation and the up/down gap at each point.
Largest |deviation| of the up-scale curve = 0.030 V, at 100 kPa (the curve sags below the line there).
Non-linearity = 0.030 V ÷ 3.98 V × 100 = 0.75 %FS. In pressure terms, 0.030 ÷ 0.0199 = 1.5 kPa.
Hysteresis: the largest down − up gap is 2.02 − 1.98 = 0.04 V, at 100 kPa. As %FS: 0.04 ÷ 3.98 × 100 = 1.0 %FS, that is 0.04 ÷ 0.0199 = 2.0 kPa.
Certificate line: range 0–200 kPa, sensitivity 19.9 mV/kPa, zero 0.02 V, non-linearity 0.75 %FS (end-point), hysteresis 1.0 %FS, at 25 °C and 10 V supply, against the dead-weight tester.
examples.answer: S = 0.0199 V/kPa (19.9 mV/kPa); zero offset 0.02 V; largest deviation 0.030 V at 100 kPa = 0.75 %FS (1.5 kPa); hysteresis 0.04 V at 100 kPa = 1.0 %FS (2.0 kPa).

traps: Never fix a span error with the zero knob, or a zero error with the span knob. Adjust zero first, then span, then recheck zero — the two interact until both settle.
An instrument that passed a verification check has not been calibrated. Verification gives pass/fail; calibration records the deviation and its uncertainty.
The denominator of %FS is the full-scale output span, not the reading. A 0.030 V deviation is 0.75 % of the 3.98 V span but about 1.5 % of the 1.98 V reading where it occurs.
Hysteresis and non-linearity are separate numbers. Hysteresis compares up-scale with down-scale at the same input; non-linearity compares one sweep with the fitted straight line.

quiz.q: Name the seven SI base units and give the symbol of each.
quiz.a: Metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

quiz.q: State the difference between calibration and adjustment, and say which comes first.
quiz.a: Calibration compares output with a known input and records the deviation; adjustment moves the zero and span trims to reduce it. Calibrate first, adjust, then calibrate again.

quiz.q: A datasheet gives pressure sensitivity as 19.9 mV/kPa. Express it in V/psi. Take 1 psi = 6.89476 kPa.
quiz.a: 19.9 mV/kPa × 6.89476 kPa/psi = 137.2 mV/psi = 0.1372 V/psi. The kPa units cancel, leaving mV per psi.

quiz.q: Distinguish primary, secondary and working standards, with one example of each.
quiz.a: Primary: national standards that realise the SI unit, kept by the national institute and used only to calibrate secondary standards (caesium clock, Josephson voltage array). Secondary: checked against the primary, held by calibration laboratories (standard resistor, Zener reference). Working: used daily on field instruments and checked against a secondary standard (dead-weight tester, process calibrator).

quiz.q: Express 1 Pa in SI base units and confirm by dimensional check that N/m² is a pressure.
quiz.a: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², so 1 N/m² = 1 kg·m·s⁻²·m⁻² = 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². Force per area, so it is a pressure, and 1 Pa = 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻².

quiz.q: A sensor repeats its readings to within 0.1 % but its calibration certificate expired three years ago. What may and may not be claimed about its accuracy?
quiz.a: Repeatability (precision) of 0.1 % may be claimed because it was measured now. Accuracy may not: the link to a primary standard has lapsed, so there is no valid uncertainty and no proof the error has not drifted. Traceability is a claim with a date.

quiz.q: Why must temperature, supply voltage and mounting torque be held constant during calibration, and why must their values appear on the certificate?
quiz.a: They are influencing inputs; the output responds to them as well as to the measurand, so varying them folds their effect into the recorded deviation. Holding them constant makes the calibration valid only at those conditions, so the certificate must state them; otherwise a later field deviation cannot be blamed on sensor or environment.

beyond: Not for the exam. Digital calibration certificates are replacing paper ones, and smart sensors keep their coefficients and calibration date in memory, so the chain travels inside the device. In audited industry and in hospitals, an out-of-tolerance calibration forces a review of every result measured since the last good one. Search next for ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation and digital calibration certificates.
